claim: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease that affects more than 300 million people worldwide.
source: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways that affects more than 300 million people worldwide (Pawankar, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pawankar, 2014.

claim: The asthmatic airway is characterised by increased airway smooth muscle (ASM) mass, sub-epithelial fibrosis and goblet cell hyperplasia/hypersecretion.
source: The asthmatic airway is characterised by numerous structural changes (collectively referred to as 'airway remodelling') including increased airway smooth muscle (ASM) mass, sub-epithelial fibrosis and goblet cell hyperplasia/hypersecretion.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about asthma pathology.

claim: Approximately half of all patients with asthma do not exhibit eosinophilic inflammation.
source: However, approximately half of all patients with asthma do not exhibit eosinophilic inflammation, and accordingly, other asthma phenotypes have been described that include neutrophilic, mixed granulocytic and paucigranulocytic inflammatory phenotypes (Simpson et al., 2006;Hinks et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Simpson et al., 2006 and Hinks et al., 2016.

claim: Paucigranulocytic asthma occurs in the absence of pronounced eosinophilia or neutrophilia.
source: Paucigranulocytic asthma occurs in the absence of pronounced eosinophilia or neutrophilia and in the few studies performed to date, is reported to affect between 32% and 52% of patients with asthma (Simpson et al., 2006; Schleich et al., 2013; Simpson et al., 2007; Porsbjerg et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Paucigranulocytic asthma affects between 32% and 52% of patients with asthma.
source: Paucigranulocytic asthma occurs in the absence of pronounced eosinophilia or neutrophilia and in the few studies performed to date, is reported to affect between 32% and 52% of patients with asthma (Simpson et al., 2006; Schleich et al., 2013; Simpson et al., 2007; Porsbjerg et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Wheezy preschool children displayed ASM remodelling prior to their diagnosis of asthma as school aged children.
source: Interestingly, O'Reilly and colleagues (O'Reilly et al., 2013) showed that wheezy preschool children displayed ASM remodelling prior to their diagnosis of asthma as school aged children.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to O'Reilly et al., 2013.

claim: Epidemiological studies have documented an association between severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection early in life and asthma development.
source: Consistent with this notion, epidemiological studies have documented an association between severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection early in life and asthma development (James et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to James et al., 2013.

claim: Persistent RSV-induced wheezing before 3 years of age is associated with chronic asthma persisting into adulthood.
source: Indeed, persistent RSV-induced wheezing before 3 years of age is associated with chronic asthma persisting into adulthood (Taussig et al., 1989; Wright et al., 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Taussig et al., 1989 and Wright et al., 1989.

claim: Tlr7-/- mice display the cardinal features of asthma following an earlier life and later life infection with pneumonia virus of mice (PVM).
source: For example, we have previously shown that Tlr7-/- mice display the cardinal features of asthma following an earlier life and later life infection with pneumonia virus of mice (PVM; a murine analogue of RSV) (Kaiko et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kaiko et al., 2013.

claim: TLR7 function is reduced in adolescents with asthma compared to non-asthmatic individuals.
source: This is consistent with the observation that, compared to non-asthmatic individuals, TLR7 function is reduced in adolescents with asthma (Roponen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Roponen et al., 2010.

claim: Increased levels of HMGB1 have been detected in the sputum of patients with asthma.
source: Increased levels of HMGB1 have been detected in the sputum of patients with asthma and high levels of HMGB1 have been associated with reduced lung function (Hou et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hou et al., 2011.

claim: High levels of HMGB1 have been associated with reduced lung function.
source: Increased levels of HMGB1 have been detected in the sputum of patients with asthma and high levels of HMGB1 have been associated with reduced lung function (Hou et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hou et al., 2011.

claim: A non-synonymous variant (rs2070600) in the AGER gene is a strong determinant of serum sRAGE levels.
source: Of note, a non-synonymous variant (rs2070600) in the AGER gene (which encodes RAGE) is a strong determinant of serum sRAGE levels (Jang et al., 2007; Maruthur et al., 2015), with the rs2070600:C allele (encoding a Gly at position 82) being associated with increased sRAGE.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jang et al., 2007 and Maruthur et al., 2015.

claim: The rs2070600:C allele is associated with increased sRAGE.
source: Of note, a non-synonymous variant (rs2070600) in the AGER gene (which encodes RAGE) is a strong determinant of serum sRAGE levels (Jang et al., 2007; Maruthur et al., 2015), with the rs2070600:C allele (encoding a Gly at position 82) being associated with increased sRAGE.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jang et al., 2007 and Maruthur et al., 2015.

claim: The rs2070600:C allele is associated with decreased risk of allergic asthma (OR = 0.87, p=0.003).
source: This same allele is associated with decreased risk of allergic asthma (OR = 0.87, p=0.003 in [Ferreira et al., 2014]).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ferreira et al., 2014.

claim: rs2070600:C is associated with decreased FEV1/FVC ratio.
source: This prediction is complicated by the apparently conflicting observation that rs2070600:C (which results in increased sRAGE) is associated with decreased FEV1/FVC ratio. However, it is important to note that this analysis was performed in the general population (Repapi et al., 2010), and hence cannot be associated with asthma or allergic disease.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Repapi et al., 2010.

claim: RAGE deficiency or HMGB1 neutralisation ameliorates type-2 inflammation in preclinical models of allergic asthma.
source: Intriguingly, RAGE deficiency or HMGB1 neutralisation ameliorates type-2 inflammation in preclinical models of allergic asthma (Ullah et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ullah et al., 2014.

claim: RAGE deficiency impairs anti-viral immunity during an early-life infection with pneumonia virus of mice (PVM).
source: Here, we show that RAGE deficiency impairs anti-viral immunity during an early-life infection with pneumonia virus of mice (PVM; a murine analogue of RSV).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Infected RAGE deficient mice had significantly higher levels of PVM RNA seven days post-infection compared to infected WT mice.
source: Infected RAGE deficient mice had significantly higher levels of PVM RNA seven dpi compared to infected WT mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: RAGE deficient mice displayed a significantly higher percentage of PVM infected airway epithelial cells (AECs) in the respiratory tract compared to WT mice at seven days post-infection.
source: RAGE deficient mice displayed a significantly higher percentage of PVM infected airway epithelial cells (AECs) in the respiratory tract compared to WT mice at seven dpi (Figure 1B & C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice had significantly lower levels of IFNα, IFNλ and IFNγ in the BAL fluid and lungs at seven days post-infection.
source: This increased infection was associated with lower levels of IFNα, IFNλ and IFNγ in the BAL fluid and lungs at seven dpi in PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice (Figure 1D & Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA and qPCR data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: There was no significant difference in IFN production between mock- and PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice.
source: Interestingly, there was no significant difference in IFN production between mock- and PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice, suggesting that RAGE deficient mice were unable to mount an IFN response following infection with PVM (p>0.999).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice had significantly lower expression of interferon regulatory factor (IRF7) relative to WT mice.
source: Consistent with this notion, PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice had significantly lower expression of interferon regulatory factor (IRF7) (which regulates IFNα production) relative to WT mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: pDCs derived from RAGE deficient mice express GFP, indicating that wild-type lung pDCs express RAGE.
source: Using flow cytometry, we demonstrated that pDCs derived from RAGE deficient mice were GFP+, indicating that under normal circumstances, wild-type lung pDCs express RAGE (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: At seven days post-infection, there were significantly fewer pDCs in the lungs of PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice compared to PVM-infected WT mice.
source: At seven dpi, there were significantly fewer pDCs in the lungs of PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice compared to PVM-infected WT mice (Figure 1G), and similar to the IFN response, there was no significant difference in pDC recruitment between mock- and PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice (Figure 1G) (p=0.6769).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice had significantly higher levels of HMGB1 in the BAL fluid compared to both mock-infected RAGE deficient mice and PVM-infected WT mice.
source: In contrast, PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice had significantly higher levels of HMGB1 in the BAL fluid compared to both mock-infected RAGE deficient mice and PVM-infected WT mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice had significantly higher levels of cytoplasmic HMGB1 in AECs compared to the other treatment groups.
source: PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice also had significantly higher levels of cytoplasmic HMGB1 in AECs compared to the other treatment groups (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was significantly more ASM mass in PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice compared to mock-infected RAGE deficient mice and PVM-infected WT mice.
source: Indeed, there was significantly more ASM mass in PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice compared to mock-infected RAGE deficient mice and PVM-infected WT mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Daily treatment of PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice with anti-HMGB1 antibody significantly decreased the levels of extracellular HMGB1 in the BAL fluid.
source: Daily treatment of PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice with anti-HMGB1 antibody (50 μg) from 2 to 6 dpi significantly decreased the levels of extracellular HMGB1 in the BAL fluid (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: The number of AECs positive for cytoplasmic HMGB1 was significantly decreased following anti-HMGB1 treatment.
source: The number of AECs positive for cytoplasmic HMGB1 was also significantly decreased following anti-HMGB1 treatment (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ASM mass was significantly lower in RAGE deficient mice that received anti-HMGB1 compared to isotype control antibody.
source: Importantly, ASM mass was significantly lower in RAGE deficient mice that received anti-HMGB1 compared to isotype control antibody (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Anti-HMGB1 significantly reduced the viral infection in the lungs of RAGE deficient mice.
source: Anti-HMGB1 also significantly reduced the viral infection in the lungs of RAGE deficient mice (Figure 3D), and significantly increased IFNα4 and IFNγ expression in the lung compared to mice treated with the isotype control (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Anti-HMGB1 significantly increased IFNα4 and IFNγ expression in the lung compared to mice treated with the isotype control.
source: Anti-HMGB1 also significantly reduced the viral infection in the lungs of RAGE deficient mice (Figure 3D), and significantly increased IFNα4 and IFNγ expression in the lung compared to mice treated with the isotype control (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There was no significant difference in viral load between PVM-infected RAGE/TLR4 deficient mice and PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice at seven days post-infection.
source: There was no significant difference in viral load between PVM-infected RAGE/TLR4 deficient mice and PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice at seven dpi (Figure 5A) (p=0.1693).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ASM growth was attenuated in RAGE/TLR4 deficient mice compared to RAGE deficient mice.
source: However, ASM growth was attenuated in RAGE/TLR4 deficient mice compared to RAGE deficient mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Exogenous IFN-α significantly decreased viral load in AECs compared to mock-treated mice.
source: Exogenous IFN-α significantly decreased viral load in AECs compared to mock-treated mice (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Both cytoplasmic and extracellular HMGB1 were significantly decreased in IFN-treated mice.
source: Moreover, both cytoplasmic and extracellular HMGB1 were significantly decreased in IFN-treated mice, and this was associated with a significant reduction in ASM growth (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and ELISA data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: IFN treatment was associated with a significant reduction in ASM growth.
source: Moreover, both cytoplasmic and extracellular HMGB1 were significantly decreased in IFN-treated mice, and this was associated with a significant reduction in ASM growth (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: There was no significant difference in the numbers of eosinophils, neutrophils or lymphocytes between mock- and PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice.
source: Analysis of the BAL cells by differential cell count showed that there was no significant difference in the numbers of eosinophils, neutrophils or lymphocytes between mock- and PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice (Figure 7A) (p=0.1161; p=0.6107; p=0.0826 and p=0.8023).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential cell count data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: IL-5 and IL-13 levels were not significantly elevated in the PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice.
source: Consistent with the lack of an eosinophilic response, IL-5 and IL-13 levels were not significantly elevated in the PVM-infected RAGE deficient mice (Figure 7B) (p=0.7016 and p=0.9973)
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Levels of IL-17A were not elevated in RAGE deficient mice upon infection with PVM.
source: Levels of IL-17A were also not elevated in RAGE deficient mice upon infection with PVM (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: TNF-α was the only cytokine that was elevated in RAGE deficient mice upon infection with PVM.
source: Indeed, the only cytokine that was elevated in RAGE deficient mice upon infection with PVM was TNF-α (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Blocking IL-13 failed to reduce viral infection of AECs, ASM mass, or cytoplasmic HMGB1 levels in AECs.
source: Blocking IL-13 failed to reduce viral infection of AECs, ASM mass, or cytoplasmic HMGB1 levels in AECs (Figure 8B–D). (p=0.7422; p=0.8369 and p=0.4266).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 8B-D.

claim: Viral antigen could not be detected in the lungs of reinfected RAGE deficient mice at various time points post-infection.
source: In contrast to the primary infection, viral antigen could not be detected in the lungs of reinfected RAGE deficient mice at various time points post-infection, presumably as a consequence of protective immunity (Figure 9B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: There was a significant increase in mucus-secreting cells in re-infected RAGE deficient mice compared to re-infected WT mice.
source: Despite this, there was a significant increase in mucus-secreting cells in re-infected RAGE deficient mice compared to re-infected WT mice (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Re-infected RAGE deficient mice displayed significantly higher levels of cytoplasmic HMGB1 in AECs and extracellular HMGB1 compared to their WT counterparts.
source: Re-infected RAGE deficient mice also displayed significantly higher levels of cytoplasmic HMGB1 in AECs and extracellular HMGB1 compared to their WT counterparts (Figure 9D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and ELISA data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Re-infected RAGE deficient mice had more ASM mass compared to re-infected WT mice.
source: Consistent with this phenotype, re-infected RAGE deficient mice had more ASM mass compared to re-infected WT mice (Figure 9E) and increased airway resistance compared to all other treatment groups (Figure 9F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Re-infected RAGE deficient mice had increased airway resistance compared to all other treatment groups.
source: Consistent with this phenotype, re-infected RAGE deficient mice had more ASM mass compared to re-infected WT mice (Figure 9E) and increased airway resistance compared to all other treatment groups (Figure 9F).
evidence: The claim is supported by airway resistance measurements shown in Figure 9F.

claim: The number of ASM cells immunopositive for PCNA was significantly increased in re-infected RAGE deficient mice at three days post-infection compared to re-infected WT mice.
source: The number of ASM cells immunopositive for proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA; a marker of active cell replication) was also significantly increased in re-infected RAGE deficient mice at three dpi compared to re-infected WT mice (Figure 10A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 10A and 10B.

claim: The inflammatory response in the BAL of re-infected RAGE deficient mice was comparable to WT mice and markedly lower than that of re-infected TLR7 deficient mice.
source: Similar to the primary PVM infection, the inflammatory response in the BAL (defined by the number eosinophils, neutrophils, mononuclear cells and lymphocytes) of re-infected RAGE deficient mice was comparable to WT mice and markedly lower than that of re-infected TLR7 deficient mice(Figure 11A).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential cell count data shown in Figure 11A.

claim: IL-5, IL-13, periostin and eotaxin-2 were not increased in RAGE deficient mice upon re-infection with PVM.
source: Similarly, IL-5, IL-13, periostin (a marker of type-2 inflammation) (Jia et al., 2012) and eotaxin-2 were not increased in RAGE deficient mice upon re-infection with PVM (Figure 11B & C) (p=0.8815, p>0.9999 and p>0.9999).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 11B and 11C.

claim: An increase in CXCL1(KC) was observed in the lungs upon re-infection in RAGE deficient mice, but this response was significantly lower than that of WT mice.
source: Whilst an increase in CXCL1(KC) was observed in the lungs upon re-infection in RAGE deficient mice, this response was significantly lower than that of WT mice (Figure 11C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 11C.

claim: Anti-HMGB1 significantly decreased the levels of cytoplasmic HMGB1 in AECs at seven days post-infection compared to treatment with the isotype control.
source: Anti-HMGB1 significantly decreased the levels of cytoplasmic HMGB1 in AECs at seven dpi compared to treatment with the isotype control (Figure 12B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 12B.

claim: Anti-HMGB1 treated RAGE deficient mice displayed significantly reduced goblet cell hyperplasia, ASM mass and AHR compared to control treated RAGE deficient mice.
source: Importantly, anti-HMGB1 treated RAGE deficient mice also displayed significantly reduced goblet cell hyperplasia, ASM mass and AHR compared to control treated RAGE deficient mice (Figure 12C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and airway resistance data shown in Figures 12C-E.

claim: Re-infected RAGE/TLR4 deficient mice had significantly fewer mucus secreting cells in the lung and displayed reduced ASM mass seven days post-infection compared to re-infected RAGE deficient mice.
source: Re-infected RAGE/TLR4 deficient mice had significantly fewer mucus secreting cells in the lung and displayed reduced ASM mass seven dpi compared to re-infected RAGE deficient mice (Figure 13A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 13A and 13B.

claim: Goblet cell hyperplasia, ASM mass and AHR were elevated in RAGE deficient mice compared to WT mice at 21 days after re-infection.
source: Goblet cell hyperplasia, ASM mass and AHR were elevated in RAGE deficient mice compared to WT mice (Figure 13D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and airway resistance data shown in Figures 13D-F.

claim: These features were absent in RAGE/TLR4 deficient mice at 21 days after re-infection.
source: Once again, these features were absent in RAGE/TLR4 deficient mice (Figure 13D–F), suggesting that TLR4 plays an important role in the development of the observed asthma phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and airway resistance data shown in Figures 13D-F.

claim: This model represents the first mouse model that recapitulates the cardinal features of paucigranulocytic asthma.
source: Thus, this model represents, to the best of our knowledge, the first mouse model that recapitulates the cardinal features of paucigranulocytic asthma.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: HMGB1 can induce smooth muscle proliferation in vitro.
source: HMGB1 can induce smooth muscle proliferation in vitro (Porto et al., 2006), suggesting that HMGB1 is capable of mediating ASM growth in the absence of any other intermediary signalling molecule.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Porto et al., 2006.

claim: HMGB1 can inhibit IFN-α production by pDCs in response to CpG containing DNA.
source: However, HMGB1 can inhibit IFN-α production by pDCs in response to CpG containing DNA (Lotze and Tracey, 2005), highlighting an important role for HMGB1 in regulating type I interferon responses.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lotze and Tracey, 2005.

claim: Several viruses and bacteria implicated in the pathogenesis of asthma are known to induce HMGB1.
source: Interestingly, several of the viruses and bacteria that have been implicated in the pathogenesis of asthma are also known to induce HMGB1 (Moisy et al., 2012; Hou et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2004, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Moisy et al., 2012; Hou et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2004, 1999.

claim: HMGB1 was common to the pathogenesis of house dust mite- and cockroach-induced allergic asthma in mice.
source: Similarly, we previously identified that HMGB1 was common to the pathogenesis of house dust mite- and cockroach-induced allergic asthma in mice (Ullah et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ullah et al., 2014.

claim: When the cysteine in location C106 is in the reduced thiol form and C23 and C45 are involved in a disulphide bridge, HMGB1 functions as a TLR4 ligand.
source: Specifically, when the cysteine in location C106 is in the reduced thiol form and C23 and C45 are involved in a disulphide bridge (HMGB1C23–C45C106h, disulphide HMGB1), HMGB1 functions as a TLR4 ligand (Yang et al., 2012, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2012, 2010.

claim: The protective anti-HMGB1 antibody used in the present study blocks all-thiol and disulphide HMGB1.
source: This is consistent with the fact that the protective anti-HMGB1 antibody used in the present study blocks all-thiol and disulphide HMGB1 (Yang et al., 2010, 2012; Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2010, 2012; Zhu et al., 2015.

claim: RAGE deficient mice produce lower levels of both type-1 and type-2 cytokines in an ovalbumin model of allergic asthma.
source: Others have demonstrated that RAGE deficient mice produce lower levels of both type-1 and type-2 cytokines in an ovalbumin model of allergic asthma (Akirav et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Akirav et al., 2014.

claim: Type-2 eosinophilic inflammation, induced in response to either house dust mite or cockroach sensitisation/challenge, is significantly reduced in the absence of RAGE.
source: Similarly, we have previously shown that type-2 eosinophilic inflammation, induced in response to either house dust mite or cockroach sensitisation/challenge, is significantly reduced in the absence of RAGE (Ullah et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ullah et al., 2014.

claim: RAGE is necessary for the lung infiltration of type-2 innate lymphoid cells.
source: However, it is noteworthy that RAGE is necessary for the lung infiltration of type-2 innate lymphoid cells (Oczypok et al., 2015), a cell type that is increasingly implicated in the priming and amplification of type two immunity (Oliphant et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Oczypok et al., 2015 and Oliphant et al., 2014.

claim: The absence of RAGE is associated with reduced neutrophil recruitment.
source: Similarly, the absence of a pronounced neutrophilic response in re-infected RAGE deficient mice is consistent with the role of RAGE in neutrophil recruitment (Orlova et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Orlova et al., 2007.

claim: HMGB1 levels have never been thoroughly investigated in paucigranulocytic asthma.
source: The mechanism of airway hyperreactivity and remodelling in these patients remains unclear, and indeed HMGB1 levels, although known to be elevated in eosinophilic asthma (Watanabe et al., 2011) have never been thoroughly investigated in in paucigranulocytic asthma.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: HMGB1 levels are known to be elevated in eosinophilic asthma.
source: The mechanism of airway hyperreactivity and remodelling in these patients remains unclear, and indeed HMGB1 levels, although known to be elevated in eosinophilic asthma (Watanabe et al., 2011) have never been thoroughly investigated in in paucigranulocytic asthma.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Watanabe et al., 2011.

claim: The elevated viral load in RAGE deficient mice was associated with the release of high mobility group box-1 (HMGB1).
source: The elevated viral load was associated with the release of high mobility group box-1 (HMGB1) which triggered airway smooth muscle remodelling in early-life.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: HMGB1 triggered airway smooth muscle remodelling in early-life.
source: The elevated viral load was associated with the release of high mobility group box-1 (HMGB1) which triggered airway smooth muscle remodelling in early-life.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Re-infection with PVM in later-life induced many of the cardinal features of asthma in the absence of eosinophilic or neutrophilic inflammation.
source: Re-infection with PVM in later-life induced many of the cardinal features of asthma in the absence of eosinophilic or neutrophilic inflammation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Anti-HMGB1 mitigated both early-life viral disease and asthma-like features.
source: Anti-HMGB1 mitigated both early-life viral disease and asthma-like features, highlighting HMGB1 as a possible novel therapeutic target.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The majority of asthma cases begin in early childhood.
source: The majority of asthma cases begin in early childhood.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about asthma.

claim: Wheeze in children is often associated with a lower respiratory tract infection.
source: Wheeze in children is often associated with a lower respiratory tract infection, raising the possibility that paediatric viral infections contribute to airway remodelling in early life and the subsequent development of asthma in later life.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about childhood wheeze.

claim: HMGB1 is an alarmin that acts as a non-histone nuclear protein in quiescent cells.
source: HMGB1 is an alarmin that acts as a non-histone nuclear protein in quiescent cells.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about HMGB1.

claim: Upon cell stimulation, HMGB1 becomes phosphorylated and is translocated from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
source: Upon cell stimulation (such as by the presence of a pathogen) HMGB1 becomes phosphorylated and is translocated from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about HMGB1 biology.

claim: Extracellular HMGB1 can bind to receptors such as RAGE, TLR2 and TLR4, and trigger a pro-inflammatory response.
source: Upon release, extracellular HMGB1 can bind to receptors such as RAGE, toll-like receptor (TLR) two and TLR4, and trigger a pro-inflammatory response (Lotze and Tracey, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lotze and Tracey, 2005.

claim: RAGE is expressed as membrane-bound (mRAGE) and soluble (sRAGE) forms.
source: This receptor is expressed as membrane-bound (mRAGE) and soluble (sRAGE) forms; the latter is produced primarily by shedding of mRAGE (Raucci et al., 2008) and is thought to function as a 'decoy' receptor, preventing RAGE ligands from interacting with mRAGE, which would normally trigger inflammation (Schmidt, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Raucci et al., 2008 and Schmidt, 2015.

claim: sRAGE is produced primarily by shedding of mRAGE.
source: This receptor is expressed as membrane-bound (mRAGE) and soluble (sRAGE) forms; the latter is produced primarily by shedding of mRAGE (Raucci et al., 2008) and is thought to function as a 'decoy' receptor, preventing RAGE ligands from interacting with mRAGE, which would normally trigger inflammation (Schmidt, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Raucci et al., 2008.

claim: sRAGE is thought to function as a 'decoy' receptor, preventing RAGE ligands from interacting with mRAGE.
source: This receptor is expressed as membrane-bound (mRAGE) and soluble (sRAGE) forms; the latter is produced primarily by shedding of mRAGE (Raucci et al., 2008) and is thought to function as a 'decoy' receptor, preventing RAGE ligands from interacting with mRAGE, which would normally trigger inflammation (Schmidt, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schmidt, 2015.

claim: pDCs are major producers of IFNα during infection.
source: pDCs are major producers of IFNα during infection (Tailor et al., 2006) and previous studies have demonstrated that RAGE plays a key role in the mobilisation of these cells in mice (Manfredi et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tailor et al., 2006.

claim: RAGE plays a key role in the mobilisation of pDCs in mice.
source: pDCs are major producers of IFNα during infection (Tailor et al., 2006) and previous studies have demonstrated that RAGE plays a key role in the mobilisation of these cells in mice (Manfredi et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Manfredi et al., 2008.

claim: Day seven was selected as the time point of interest because this represents the peak of PVM replication in mice.
source: Day seven was selected as the time point of interest, as this represents the peak of PVM replication in mice (Kaiko et al., 2013; Bonville et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kaiko et al., 2013 and Bonville et al., 2006.

claim: qPCR cannot differentiate between infectious and non-infectious viral particles.
